transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-29
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO - HalcyonPay), Elena Moreno (Head of Platform), Samir Khan (SRE)

Summary (auto):
Post-incident workshop to align on root cause of Nov 26 latency surge, validate mitigations (batching, cache, autoscaler tuning), review SLA shielding options (circuit breakers, model fallback, dedicated pool), and agree next steps for benchmarks and remediation timeline.

Topics:
- Incident timeline and immediate mitigations applied
- Root cause hypotheses (autoscaler, bursty traffic, KV cache cold start, model variant mismatch)
- Proposed shielding: dedicated reserved pool, regional fallback, model quantization + perf tradeoffs
- Security/compliance notes for logs and replay data sharing

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time, uh, we'll run for about an hour plus. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:00:12] Ravi: Yeah, loud and clear. We mostly want to walk away with a concrete short list of mitigations and a benchmark plan.
[00:00:20] Maya: Perfect. Diego from our infra team will pick up the deep perf stuff. Diego, want to intro high-level?
[00:00:30] Diego: Sure. Hi all. We looked at the trace you sent, the surge on 11/26 shows a p99 latency jump from ~320ms to nearly 1.8s for a 22-minute window. There were also a lot of request retries which amplified load.
[00:00:45] Samir: Right, we saw retries from our side — client library retried a few times by default, that made it worse. But even ignoring retries there was a step increase.
[00:00:55] Elena: To be clear, we were on hosted plan with the shared pool, not dedicated. We had a big marketing push that day; traffic spiked 4x.
[00:01:05] Maya: Okay that's important. Shared pool + bursty multi-tenant traffic often increases tail latency if the runtime can't fast-path batching.
[00:01:15] Diego: Two immediate hypotheses: 1) KV cache cold start and ineffective prefix caching under the traffic pattern, 2) autoscaler lag because the burst was very sudden and the pod spin-up took longer than expected. There's also a third factor - model memory pressure caused kernel thrash on old GPU instances.
[00:01:31] Ravi: You mentioned KV cache, we call it the prefix cache. Is that something we can make sticky for our tenant?
[00:01:39] Diego: On hosted shared pools we rely on adaptive caching. For strict stickiness you'd need a dedicated pool or partitioning. We can prioritize your traffic but tenancy isolation comes with reserved capacity.
[00:01:50] Elena: Dedicated is possible but we need cost numbers and a fallback for when reserved is exhausted. We can't just pay for peak all the time.
[00:01:59] Maya: Totally understandable. We've got a few levers: reserved capacity (Dedicated), regional fallback to a lower-cost model variant, or a graceful degradation strategy (partial responses, rate limiting). We'll map cost vs latency.
[00:02:12] Samir: Also, the autoscaler. We saw many cold starts. Can we tune the scale-up aggressiveness or have warm standby?
[00:02:20] Diego: Yes — autoscaler policy can be tuned per-customer in Dedicated; in Hosted we have per-route burst buffers but they are global. For immediate mitigation we can recommend a smaller min replica (for dedicated) or pre-warm policies.
[00:02:33] Ravi: Right, but in hosted we can't change min replica. So what's the fastest short-term fix?
[00:02:38] Diego: Short-term: 1) apply client-side retry/backoff changes to avoid amplification, 2) short TTL for prefix cache warming, 3) enable model fallback to a lower-latency variant for tail requests.
[00:02:50] Elena: Model fallback - does that change response quality? We have compliance concerns if results degrade.
[00:02:57] Maya: Good point. Fallbacks can be tested with canary routing — e.g., 5% of tail traffic goes to the cheaper variant. We monitor quality with your prompt set; Redwood Optimize can flag regressions.
[00:03:08] Ravi: We need a clear guardrail: if fallback leads to >2% quality regression on key prompts, auto-rollback.
[00:03:14] Diego: We can implement a quality gate tied to the eval suite you provide. If it crosses threshold, the routing should revert.
[00:03:20] Samir: On the data sharing: you asked for logs and traces; we can upload sanitized traces but need to ensure PII is stripped. Any compliance concerns on Redwood side?
[00:03:30] Maya: We're SOC 2 compliant and we support encrypted S3 uploads for traces; we also support short-lived presigned links. We'll flag any sensitive fields you mark.
[00:03:38] Elena: Great. We'll sanitize and share. I'll own that.
[00:03:43] Maya: Note in the follow-up I'll drop a drive link and the incident timeline.
[00:03:49] Diego: Back to root cause, there's a component we haven't discussed: request shaping from the client library. If the SDK retries immediately on 429s, it creates spikes. Samir, can you confirm your client defaults?
[00:03:58] Samir: Yeah, default is 3 retries with linear backoff. We can change to exponential + jitter, but we wanted to confirm that it won't hide transient errors.
[00:04:08] Maya: Exponential + jitter is industry best practice and reduces thundering herd. We can provide sample retry policy.
[00:04:13] Ravi: Can Redwood simulate the incoming burst in a replay so we can reproduce on a dedicated pool?
[00:04:19] Diego: Yup — if you provide the traffic replay (sanitized), we can replay it against a dedicated cluster to show whether the problem persists. That will also let us measure cold-start contribution.
[00:04:30] Elena: What's the estimated time to run that internal repro?
[00:04:34] Diego: With prepared telemetry it takes ~48 hours to spin up and run systematic tests and collect p50/p95/p99 across variants. We'll aim for a 3-5 day window including analysis.
[00:04:43] Maya: We'll commit to that if you can share workload by 12/02.
[00:04:47] Ravi: Ok. We can try to get it by then.
[00:04:50] Samir: On the autoscaler tuning, are there quick flags we can change in hosted? Or do we need to move to Dedicated?
[00:04:56] Diego: Hosted has a few knobs but they're global. For customer-specific policies you want Dedicated. Also Dedicated unlocks KV cache partitioning (so your cache isn't evicted by other tenants).
[00:05:06] Elena: Cost sensitivity check: half our traffic is non-critical (internal diffs) - could we route non-critical to a cheaper model automatically?
[00:05:14] Maya: Yes — route classification before hitting the LLM (edge classifier) or annotate requests so Redwood routing splits by importance. That reduces cost while keeping critical paths low-latency.
[00:05:24] Ravi: That seems promising. We'll need guidance on how to classify reliably.
[00:05:28] Diego: We can provide a starter classifier and a split-testing deck.
[00:05:32] Elena: Security question: when you run dedicated on our VPC, how do you handle keys and logs? We need KMS integration and audit trails.
[00:05:40] Maya: For Private/Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS and provide audit logs with SSO/RBAC enforcement. We'll include the security pack in the follow-up.
[00:05:49] Samir: Good. Also we saw a few 5xxs in the window. Were those internal Redwood errors or upstream?
[00:05:55] Diego: Mixed. Some were internal timeouts hitting the model runtime; others were client errors from malformed payloads during the surge. We'll annotate those in the timeline.
[00:06:04] Maya: Okay let's pivot to an action matrix — immediate, near-term (1-2 weeks), long-term (quarter).
[00:06:10] Diego: Immediate (this week): change client retry policy, add short-term rate limit at edge, and provide incident timeline and raw traces.
[00:06:18] Maya: Near-term (1-2 weeks): run replay on Dedicated, test model fallback canary, tune autoscaler or move to reserved pool; also surface cost estimates for reserved capacity.
[00:06:26] Elena: Long-term: consider dedicated pool or Private deployment if traffic patterns justify it and map ROI. Also work on request classification and rollout of graceful degradation.
[00:06:35] Ravi: Who owns cost estimates?
[00:06:38] Maya: I'll own cost estimates and will include multiple sizing options and cost per month and projected savings for caching/quantization.
[00:06:46] Samir: Can we get a prioritized list of mitigations that are low-effort/high-impact?
[00:06:50] Diego: Sure — 1) client retry change (low), 2) enable model fallback canary (low-medium), 3) pre-warm min replicas (medium, requires Dedicated), 4) KV cache partitioning (medium, Dedicated).
[00:07:02] Elena: Let's talk about quantization. Does that materially reduce latency? We worry about quality fallout.
[00:07:08] Diego: Quantization can reduce memory and inference latency for certain model families. But it sometimes changes tokenization behavior subtly. We'll run quality evals on your prompt set before recommending.
[00:07:18] Ravi: Any immediate risks with trying quantized variants in canary?
[00:07:22] Maya: Risk is quality regression. We'll gate it behind your eval pass threshold.
[00:07:26] Samir: I want to call out that our incident had a big region-specific component — APAC region saw much higher latencies than US. Any routing suggestions?
[00:07:35] Diego: Yes — smart routing by region can help. Also using regional caches and making sure the model variant compiled for the region's hardware selection. We can verify compilation/kernels per region.
[00:07:46] Elena: Can you provide a per-region perf heatmap for the last 90 days?
[00:07:50] Diego: We'll generate that and include with the perf spreadsheet.
[00:07:54] Maya: Quick questions from Ravi earlier about SLA language — you asked for shielding such that tail events won't breach our SLA without fallback. What's reasonable?
[00:08:03] Diego: Technically, a combination of reserved baseline plus fallback policy can keep p99 inside targets. We can propose an SLA amendment that includes a dedicated baseline of X qps and fallback triggers.
[00:08:15] Ravi: We'll need legal to weigh in but that sounds workable.
[00:08:19] Maya: Action item: I'll draft a proposed SLA amendment and share with your procurement/legal.
[00:08:25] Elena: Please include rollback clauses and a test schedule.
[00:08:29] Maya: Will do.
[00:08:32] Diego: A few gotchas to call out: on some older GPU families the kernel selection causes variance for long sequences — if you have workloads with long contexts that hits memory thrash. We should validate your typical context length distribution.
[00:08:44] Samir: Average is 1.2k tokens but occasional 8k for fraud cases.
[00:08:49] Diego: That 8k tail could be driving memory pressure. For those, a larger GPU or a split model approach may be necessary.
[00:08:57] Elena: So the plan is — we share workload by 12/02, Redwood runs replay and returns perf sheet by ~12/05, then we review and decide dedicated pilot or config changes?
[00:09:08] Maya: Yes, that's accurate. We'll also share a short checklist for sanitization and the drive link.
[00:09:13] Ravi: Can you include an estimate of rollback risk if we switch to Dedicated mid-Q4?
[00:09:18] Maya: We'll include migration steps and estimated downtime (should be zero with blue/green), but data residency and network setup could take lead time.
[00:09:27] Samir: One more thing — during the incident, our monitoring showed increased GC on the service that posts to Redwood. Could that have introduced request bursts?
[00:09:36] Diego: Possibly; upstream batching effects can cause sudden bursts. Part of the replay should capture client-side inter-arrival times to reproduce that.
[00:09:45] Elena: Ok — we will log inter-arrival and attach to the upload.
[00:09:50] Maya: Recap and owners: Maya to share timeline and cost estimates; Diego to run repro and perf analysis; Elena to upload sanitized workload; Samir to pull autoscaler logs; Ravi to coordinate legal review for SLA amendment.
[00:10:07] Ravi: Fine. Can we schedule the follow-up slot now?
[00:10:10] Maya: Let's tentatively book 2026-12-08 for the benchmark review at the same time. I'll send an invite.
[00:10:18] Elena: Works for us.
[00:10:20] Diego: Quick note on monitoring hooks — we'll provide tracing instrumentation snippets to add correlation IDs and KV cache metrics to make future triage faster.
[00:10:29] Samir: Please do, that'll help.
[00:10:32] Maya: Any blockers or open questions we haven't covered?
[00:10:36] Ravi: Not from me, main thing is getting the sanitized traces by 12/02.
[00:10:40] Elena: We'll queue that up.
[00:10:42] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the drive link, and you'll see the perf plan and cost options in the deck.
[00:10:49] Diego: One more micro-point — consider enabling a short-term adaptive circuit breaker at the API gateway to shed non-critical traffic during tail events; that can reduce the blast radius immediately.
[00:10:59] Samir: We'll discuss that with our infra team.
[00:11:02] Maya: Okay closing notes — I will send the recap, action items and the drive link. Follow-up benchmark review on 2026-12-08. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:12] Ravi: Thanks all.

(Transcription notes: occasional words misheard, e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache", "V P C" for VPC, and model names redacted; timestamps provided every ~30-90s. Some fragments omitted for brevity; full audio available.)

Shared artifacts referenced: incident timeline (link: https://drive.redwood.internal/halcyonpay/incident-1126), perf template (link: https://sheets.redwood/internal/perf-templates/halcyonpay), security pack (link: https://docs.redwood/internal/security-pack).

End of transcript.
